title: Prototype systems for rechargeable magnesium batteries
section: 1.1. Magnesium and lithium require different electrolyte logic
paragraph_text: The electrolyte problem in a magnesium battery begins at the point where dissolved magnesium must become metal. Aurbach and colleagues' prototype established that an organohaloaluminate electrolyte could support both reversible magnesium deposition and insertion into a Chevrel-phase positive electrode.[1,2,3] Subsequent progress has produced organoboron formulations, inorganic chloride complexes and chemically distinct boron-based salts, expanding the available coordination chemistry without removing the difficulty of combining metal compatibility with useful positive-electrode operation.[4,5,6,7] The defining challenge is therefore broader than finding a liquid that conducts ions or produces a magnesium deposit. It is to identify a solution chemistry whose charge carriers can reach a productive interfacial pathway repeatedly while the same electrolyte survives exposure to both electrodes.

title: Nonaqueous Liquid Electrolytes for Lithium-Based Rechargeable Batteries
section: 1.1. Magnesium and lithium require different electrolyte logic
paragraph_text: Lithium electrolyte research supplies an extensive chemical vocabulary, but its most familiar design narrative needs qualification when applied to magnesium. In many lithium systems, increasing anion participation or decreasing free-solvent activity is useful partly because it changes the species reduced at the negative electrode and the interphase they produce.[8,9,10] Salt-rich lithium electrolytes and superconcentrated acetonitrile formulations exemplify how collective solution organisation can alter electrochemical behaviour, rather than simply changing the properties of an isolated solvent.[11,12] These observations do not establish that anion-rich shells are universally preferable even for lithium. They establish that solvation, reaction selectivity and interphase chemistry are coupled. The magnesium question is which part of that coupling remains beneficial when the transported ion is divalent and the metal is readily passivated.

Its greater charge density promotes substantial solvent polarisation, multidentate coordination and sensitivity to counterion association.[13,14] Removing one donor can reorganize the remaining shell; changing an anion can alter ligand residence times, precursor charge and the accessible interfacial configurations. title: Rechargeable magnesium battery: Current status and key challenges for the future
section: 1.2. The bottleneck is a missing description of coupled interactions
paragraph_text: Electrolyte discovery still depends heavily on recipe changes that alter several molecular and interfacial variables at once. Donor number, dielectric response, average coordination number and calculated binding energy each describe a useful aspect of a formulation. None identifies, on its own, the state that supplies magnesium to the electrode or the transformation that limits its transfer.[24,25,26,27] A stronger donor may improve dissolution while slowing ligand departure. A weaker ion pair may increase the population of charged carriers while exposing a coordinated solvent to reduction. A strongly associated precursor may be productive if its ligands rearrange readily at the surface, yet ineffective if it becomes a slowly exchanging reservoir. The same macroscopic improvement can therefore arise from different microscopic changes.

section: 1.3. Scope and central proposition
paragraph_text: We develop this argument as a testable interpretation of existing electrolyte chemistry, rather than a universal assertion that anion coordination is catalytic. Recent counterpoised-interaction and dynamic-solvation studies make the hypothesis concrete, while weak-pairing formulations supply an indispensable comparison.[23,32,33] The analysis asks when an anion-containing state lowers the relevant barrier, when it instead creates a trap, and how either outcome can be distinguished from sacrificial interphase formation. It then identifies the measurements needed to connect these molecular effects to efficient magnesium cycling and positive-electrode compatibility. The objective is a design logic that remains accountable when the salt, solvent, potential or electrode history changes.

title: A weakly ion pairing electrolyte designed for high voltage magnesium batteries
section: 2.1. Weak ion pairing opens a productive route
paragraph_text: Reducing anion participation can be effective when association stabilizes an unreactive precursor or promotes an unfavourable decomposition channel. The weakly ion-pairing Mg(TFSI)₂ electrolyte reported by Li and colleagues provides a direct example of solvent design used to facilitate pair dissociation while enabling magnesium cycling and high-voltage operation.[33] Earlier studies of TFSI-based formulations also show why a nominally convenient salt does not guarantee metal compatibility: the solvent environment and interfacial history remain decisive.[34,35,36] The transferable inference is that unnecessary association can be removed from the productive pathway. It is not that all anions should remain outside the first shell under every condition.

paragraph_text: A rational screening sequence should identify the dominant bulk populations, test their exchange dynamics, and then examine which species participate near the electrode. section: 5.2. Connecting molecular simulation to operating-cell behaviour
paragraph_text: Robustness to impurities provides a useful challenge for any transferred mechanism. A hybrid AlCl₃/MgCl₂/Mg(TFSI)₂ electrolyte has been reported to tolerate substantial introduced water while remaining active, in contrast to the sensitivity of many magnesium formulations.[99] This is evidence for that formulation's operational chemistry, not permission to treat water as irrelevant in other systems. A multiscale model should predict whether a perturbation changes precursor populations, promotes passivation or is buffered by another reaction. Testing the response to a controlled impurity addition can reveal a missing reaction branch that an apparently successful dry-electrolyte model would never encounter. Such challenges make the eventual design rule more credible in a working cell.

A negative electric field can change the local abundance and orientation of charged complexes, but electrostatic exclusion of a free anion does not prove that an anion cannot approach as part of a positively charged complex. Thus, the relevant precursor charge and its ligand identities should remain explicit when bulk populations are transferred into a surface model.[15,16,31] The model should resolve whether an anion leaves before adsorption, remains during coordination reorganization or reacts in the double layer. title: A weakly ion pairing electrolyte designed for high voltage magnesium batteries
section: 6.1. Reframing the role of the first-shell anion
paragraph_text: The distinction resolves the apparent contradiction between weak-pairing and anion-assisted electrolytes without assigning them one common microscopic mechanism. Weak pairing can remove a slowly exchanging or reactive precursor from the transfer network. Selected coordination can create a more accessible connection between solution and interfacial states. Their shared outcome is an increase in productive magnesium flux, but the chemistry that produces that outcome differs.[33,23] The important descriptor is a conditional pathway through the coupled Mg²⁺–anion–solvent landscape, interpreted together with precursor populations and competing reactions. Neither the smallest binding energy nor the largest anion coordination number is a general design target.

section: 6.3. From a molecular mechanism to a useful operating cell
paragraph_text: The practical objective is a single electrolyte that combines efficient magnesium-metal cycling with meaningful positive-electrode operation. A desolvation-promoting anion or ligand can still be oxidatively vulnerable, corrosive or excessively consumed. A stable, weakly coordinating salt can still leave solvent exchange or solid-state cathode transport too slow. The design problem therefore has several coupled constraints; it cannot be solved by optimising the negative electrode in isolation.[100,89] The appropriate endpoint is an operating envelope measured with the intended cathode, current collectors, electrolyte inventory and magnesium excess, including the composition changes that accumulate during cycling.
